3.3.3.sourceQuote: Orthogonality means “uncorrelated.” That means in an orthogonal model; all the independent variables are uncorrelated.
3.3.3.example: False positive: COVID-19 test positive though the patient is not infected.

4.1.1.title: Introduction to Hypothesis
4.1.1.quick: A hypothesis is a tentative, testable statement about a research problem that may or may not be true and must be verified empirically.
keyIdeas: “Hypo” = subject to verification; “thesis” = statement of a problem’s solution.
Unlike a theory (tested, well-substantiated explanation), a hypothesis is provisional.
Types include simple, complex, empirical/working, null, alternative, logical, and statistical.
Simple: relation between two variables (cause → effect); complex: more than two variables.
Mutual-fund illustration: H0 / H1 / H2 phrased so decisions (launch or not) follow which claim is supported.
detail: Hypothesis testing compares mutually exclusive statements about a population using sample data; a statistically significant finding means strong evidence for one of the hypotheses.

Formulation draws on hypothesis types. A simple hypothesis links one independent and one dependent variable (e.g., smoking leads to cancer). A complex hypothesis links several causes and effects. An empirical/working hypothesis starts as an assumption and becomes testable. Logical hypotheses are rationally validated (J.S. Mill’s principles). Statistical hypotheses can be verified statistically whether or not they seem logical.
4.1.1.sourceQuote: Thus, “hypothesis” is “ a tentative statement, which is subject to verification and states the solution of a problem”.
4.1.1.compare: A theory is a tested, well-substantiated explanation; a hypothesis is tentative and still requires empirical verification.
4.1.1.example: Mutual fund launch: H1 (≥20% invest) → launch; H2 (<20% invest) → do not launch.

4.1.2.title: Developing Hypothesis: Null and Alternate
4.1.2.quick: The null hypothesis (H0) states no relationship between variables; the alternative (H1) is the competing claim chosen after modifying the prior statement.
keyIdeas: Null (H0 / h0): contrary to the positive empirical claim — no relationship between dependent and independent variables.
Alternative (H1 / h1): the feasible, effective competing hypothesis after refinement.
Test statistic: estimator from sample data used for the decision.
Rejection region (RR): values of the test statistic that reject H0 in favour of H1.
Significance level (often 5% or 1%): chance of rejecting H0 when it is actually true.
detail: If the calculated test statistic falls in the rejection region, reject H0 and accept H1; if it does not, accept H0 (the non-rejection / acceptance region).

The significance level is the threshold probability for choosing between null and alternative. At 5%, the material notes a long-run risk of incorrect judgement about 5% of the time when the hypothesis is accepted at that level.
4.1.2.sourceQuote: It is contrary to the positive statement of the empirical hypothesis, which has no relationship between dependent and independent variables.
4.1.2.compare: H0 = no relationship / status quo claim; H1 = the refined competing claim you hope the data support.

4.1.3.title: Type I and Type II Error
4.1.3.quick: Type I error wrongly rejects a true H0 (wrongly accepts H1); Type II wrongly accepts a false H0 (wrongly rejects H1).
keyIdeas: Type I: H0 true but rejected; H1 wrongly accepted.
Type II: H0 false but accepted; H1 wrongly rejected.
Correct decisions: accept H0 when H0 true; accept H1 when H1 true — no error.
Children’s-channel ad example: wrong H0 rejection → skip needed ads; wrong H1 rejection → pay for unnecessary ads.
“State of nature” = the authentic situation; mistakes can arise when linking states to actions or when study findings misrepresent nature.
detail: Hypothesis pairs are designed so they cannot both be true and false at once; action 1 follows if the first hypothesis is true, action 2 if the second is true.
Decision tables map true state vs conclusion: Type I when H0 is true but you conclude H1; Type II when H1 is true but you conclude H0.
4.1.3.sourceQuote: H0 wrongly rejected and H1 wrongly accepted
4.1.3.example: H0: adults ≥20% of children’s TV audience (advertise); H1: adults <20% (don’t advertise).

4.1.4.title: One-Tailed and Two-Tailed Test
4.1.4.quick: A one-tailed test allows the alternative to go only higher or only lower than H0; a two-tailed test allows departure in either direction (≠).
keyIdeas: One-tailed: H0: μ = μ0; H1: μ < μ0 or μ > μ0 (not both at once).
Two-tailed: H0: μ = μ0; H1: μ ≠ μ0 — care about both higher and lower.
Drug example: only “more effective” matters → one-tailed setup.
Supplier strength vs target: higher or lower both matter → two-tailed.
Compare p-value to α; sign of the test statistic shows which tail.
detail: In the new-medication illustration, failing to reject H0 or rejecting in the wrong direction both stop further production/study, so a one-tailed test focuses on greater effectiveness.
For a two-sided 1-sample t-test of mean strength against a target, a negative t-value in the left critical region means the mean is smaller than the target.
4.1.4.sourceQuote: In a one-tailed test, the alternative hypothesis allows for the parameter being tested to be either bigger or less than the parameter under the null hypothesis, but not both simultaneously.
4.1.4.compare: One-tailed = directional alternative; two-tailed = non-directional (≠) alternative.

4.1.5.title: Degree of Freedom
4.1.5.quick: Degrees of freedom are how many values in a calculation are free to vary; often df = N − 1 (or observations minus parameters).
keyIdeas: Needed for validity of chi-square, t, and F tests.
General idea: df = (number of observations) − (number of parameters).
Common sample formula: Degree of Freedom = N − 1.
Example: values 15, 30, 25, 10 → mean 20 → df = 4 − 1 = 3 can vary while mean stays 20.
detail: Because df identifies how many values in the final calculation may vary, they contribute to outcome validity. Calculations often depend on sample size and parameters being estimated.
In the vaccine heart-rate illustration, df enters the significance calculation when comparing vaccinated vs not vaccinated groups.
4.1.5.sourceQuote: Degrees of freedom equal the number of values in a data set minus 1 in a statistical formula like : Degree of Freedom = N-1

4.1.6.title: Confidence Intervals
4.1.6.quick: A confidence interval is the estimate ± its variation — the range expected to contain the estimate if the study is redone at a stated confidence level.
keyIdeas: Confidence in statistics is another way to describe probability.
95% CI: expect the estimate between the bounds in 95 of 100 similar retests.
Relation: Confidence level = 1 − α (e.g., α = 0.05 → 95%).
Used for proportions, means, differences of means/proportions, and variation among groups.
Same point estimate can have a wider CI when data are more volatile.
detail: Point estimates alone give no sense of surrounding range; CIs convey the variance around the estimate.
India vs America TV-hours survey: both groups average 35 hours/week, but greater disparity among Indian respondents yields a broader CI than the American estimate.
4.1.6.sourceQuote: A confidence interval is the mean of our estimate plus and minus the variation in that estimate.
4.1.6.example: Both groups mean 35 TV hours/week; more volatile Indian responses → wider CI.

4.1.7.title: Level of Significance: The Confidence Coefficient
4.1.7.quick: The confidence coefficient (confidence level) shades the central portion of the sampling distribution (e.g., 95%) that defines the confidence interval around the sample mean.
keyIdeas: Graphically: centre the interval on the sample mean and shade the central 95% of the distribution.
That shaded range of sample means is the 95% confidence interval.
Fuel-price illustration: population mean said to fall between 267 and 394 at 95% confidence.
Ties back to α via confidence level = 1 − α from the prior section.
detail: Section 4.1.7 focuses on interpreting the confidence coefficient visually: the sampling distribution covered by 95% of sample means in the shaded range is the 95% CI for the data.
For the fuel-price example, the material states the population mean for fuel prices falls between 267 and 394 with a 95% confidence interval.
4.1.7.sourceQuote: The sampling distribution is covered by 95% of the sample means in the shaded range [267 394]. For our sample data, this range represents the 95% confidence interval.

4.1.8.title: Rejection and Non-rejection Regions
4.1.8.quick: The rejection (critical) region is all test-statistic values that reject H0; a critical value separates it from the non-rejection region.
keyIdeas: α = probability the test statistic falls in the critical region when H0 is true.
Left-tailed: H1 uses < ; right-tailed: H1 uses > ; two-tailed: H1 uses ≠ with α/2 in each tail.
Decision: z/t in rejection region → reject H0; otherwise fail to reject H0.
Failing to reject ≠ proving H0 true — only insufficient evidence to reject.
Type I probability = α; Type II probability typically denoted β.
detail: Calculate the standardised test statistic (z or t). If it falls in the rejection region, reject H0; if not, fail to reject H0.
The same section also introduces Bayesian probability as degree of certainty (0–1), prior vs posterior probabilities, and Bayes’ Box updates — complementary framing of belief revision after data.
4.1.8.sourceQuote: The critical region, also known as the rejection region, encompasses all values of the test statistic that lead to the rejection of the null hypothesis.
4.1.8.compare: Reject H0 only if the statistic is in the critical region; otherwise fail to reject (do not claim H0 proven).

4.1.9.title: Hypothesis Testing Procedure
4.1.9.quick: Hypothesis testing is a stepwise process: formulate H0/Ha, sample, choose a method, compute the statistic and p-value, compare to α, then conclude.
keyIdeas: Formulate null (no relationship) and alternative (predicted relationship).
Collect representative sample data.
Choose an appropriate testing method for the data and question.
Calculate a test statistic (e.g., z-score, t-statistic).
p-value: probability of results as extreme as observed if H0 is true.
Low p (< α) → reject H0; high p (≥ α) → fail to reject H0.
detail: Example pair: H0 — no average height difference between men and women; Ha — men are taller on average.
A low p-value suggests the observed difference is unlikely by chance alone (supports Ha); a high p-value suggests random variation (supports H0). Draw the conclusion in the research-question context.
4.1.9.sourceQuote: The p-value quantifies the probability of observing results as extreme as those obtained, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

4.1.10.title: Types of Tests
4.1.10.quick: Statistical tests for hypothesis-based inference fall into parametric (distributional assumptions) and non-parametric (fewer distribution assumptions) families.
keyIdeas: Parametric: assume normality / homogeneity of variance, etc. — e.g., t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression.
Non-parametric: no distribution assumption required — e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis.
Also categorised by research focus: quantitative (numerical) vs qualitative/categorical analysis.
Qualitative/categorical tests uncover associations among categorical variables.
detail: Parametric tests rely on assumptions about the underlying data distribution to make accurate inferences; non-parametric tests are more robust when those assumptions are violated.
Choice also depends on whether the work is quantitative or qualitative; categorical statistical tests matter for qualitative-style categorical data.
4.1.10.sourceQuote: These tests are broadly classified into two categories: parametric and non-parametric.
4.1.10.compare: Parametric needs distributional assumptions; non-parametric does not require them.

4.1.11.title: How to Select a Test
4.1.11.quick: Selecting a test follows seven steps: question → null → α → one- vs two-tailed → number of variables → data type → study design (paired vs unpaired).
keyIdeas: Define the research question that guides collection and analysis.
Formulate a null of no statistical significance.
Set the significance level in the protocol.
Choose one-tailed (clear direction) or two-tailed (no anticipated direction).
Match tests to single-variable vs multivariable problems.
Assess continuous / categorical / binary data and normality vs skew for continuous data.
Account for paired (dependent) vs unpaired (independent) designs.
detail: One-tailed tests suit clear directional evidence; two-tailed when no specific direction is anticipated.
Paired designs compare dependent samples; unpaired designs compare independent samples — this distinction drives many parametric choices later in 4.2.
4.1.11.sourceQuote: One-tailed tests are suitable when evidence points clearly in one direction, while two-tailed tests are appropriate when no specific direction is anticipated.

4.2.1.title: Important Parametric Tests
4.2.1.quick: Key parametric tests assuming normality include the t-test (small n, unknown σ), Z-test (large n or known σ), and F-test (comparing variances / ANOVA).
keyIdeas: Parametric tests assume fixed population parameters (mean, SD) and typically normal populations (CLT may justify approximate normality).
t-test (Student/Gossett): means of groups; n < 30; unknown variance; df = n − 1; one-sample, independent two-sample, paired.
Z-test: sample vs population mean when n > 30 or variance known; also large-sample two-mean comparisons.
F-test: compare variances of two samples; also central to ANOVA for ≥3 group means.
detail: Uses listed for parametric work include CIs for a mean (known or unknown σ), for variance, and for the difference of two means with unknown SD (t).
Examples in the text: paired t for BP before/after medication; Z for comparing men’s and women’s salaries; F for bolt-diameter variability across machines.
4.2.1.sourceQuote: Parametric tests are statistical tests that assume the underlying data follows a normal distribution.
4.2.1.compare: t for small samples / unknown σ; Z for large samples / known σ; F for variances (and ANOVA).

4.2.2.title: Single Population Mean Using Z-statistic
4.2.2.quick: A Z-test checks whether a sample mean differs from a known population mean when σ is known — especially useful for large samples (n > 30).
keyIdeas: Also used when the test-statistic distribution can be approximated as normal.
Applications: sample mean vs population mean; two sample means with known variances and large n (≥ 30).
One-sample Z: sample mean vs population mean.
Two-sample Z: compare means of two different samples (uses group means, population SDs, and n).
detail: The section frames Z as the large-sample / known-σ route for mean hypotheses, contrasting later with the t-route when σ is unknown and n is small.
Two-sample notation references x̄1, x̄2, σ1, σ2, and n as inputs to the standardised comparison.
4.2.2.sourceQuote: A Z-test is a statistical method used to determine whether the mean of a sample is significantly different from a known population mean when the population standard deviation is known.
4.2.2.compare: Prefer Z when σ known and/or n large; prefer t when σ unknown and n small.

4.2.3.title: Single Population Mean Using T-statistic
4.2.3.quick: The t-test uses Student’s t-distribution for mean differences when n is small (< 30) and the population standard deviation is unknown.
keyIdeas: Assumptions: normal population; random independent samples; small n; unknown σ.
One-sample t: sample mean vs known population mean.
Independent two-sample t: means of two independent samples.
Paired t: related samples (before/after).
Statistic uses sample mean, sample SD (s), n, and μ.
detail: Parametric t-testing is the small-sample counterpart to Z when σ must be estimated from the sample.
Two-sample form uses each group’s sample mean and sample SD rather than known population σ.
4.2.3.sourceQuote: It is primarily used to determine if there is a significant difference between the means of two groups, especially when the sample size is small (i.e., less than 30) and the population standard deviation is unknown.

4.2.4.title: Hypothesis Testing for Population Proportions
4.2.4.quick: Proportion tests ask whether a sample proportion differs from a hypothesised population proportion — suited to categorical data.
keyIdeas: H0: population proportion equals a specified value; Ha: differs (one- or two-tailed).
Common α choices: 0.05, 0.01, 0.10.
Large samples: Z-score test statistic from the proportion formula.
Two-tailed α = 0.05 → critical values ±1.96 on the standard normal.
Reject H0 if Z is in the rejection region; otherwise fail to reject; then conclude about Ha.
detail: Steps mirror general hypothesis testing: state hypotheses, set α, compute Z, apply the critical-value decision rule, and conclude whether evidence supports the alternative.
Focus remains conceptual: categorical proportion claims with large-sample normal (Z) critical regions.
4.2.4.sourceQuote: Hypothesis testing for population proportions involves determining whether a sample proportion significantly differs from a known or hypothesised population proportion.

4.2.5.title: Variance vs Hypothesised Population Variance
4.2.5.quick: A chi-square test compares a sample variance to a hypothesised population variance for normally distributed populations.
keyIdeas: Can be two-tailed (σ² = σ0² vs ≠), right-tailed (σ² > σ0²), or left-tailed (σ² < σ0²).
Chi-square distribution has df = n − 1; starts at zero and is asymmetric.
As df grow, the shape approaches normality.
Two-tailed α = 0.10 with 10 df: critical values ≈ 3.94 and 18.307 (α/2 = 0.05 each tail).
Reject H0 if the statistic is below the lower or above the upper critical value.
detail: Because variance cannot be negative, the chi-square curve is asymmetrical from zero upward.
Table-reading illustration: split α for two tails, look up right-tail 0.05 and 0.95 columns for the given df, then apply the dual critical-value rule.
4.2.5.sourceQuote: The chi-square test is a statistical method used to determine whether there is a significant difference between the observed variance of a sample and a hypothesised population variance.

4.2.6.title: Equality of Variances of Two Normal Populations
4.2.6.quick: The F-test (Snedecor & Cochran) compares whether two normal populations have equal variances, using the ratio of the larger sample variance to the smaller.
keyIdeas: H0 usually: variances equal; Ha: not equal (one- or two-tailed as needed).
Draw samples, compute variances and sizes; F = larger s² / smaller s².
df for numerator and denominator = each sample size − 1.
Reject H0 if calculated F exceeds the critical value.
Conditions: random samples, independent observations, approximately normal populations.
detail: Related material also covers testing a population correlation coefficient ρ via sample r (H0: ρ = 0; Ha: ρ ≠ 0) with a t-statistic on n − 2 df — significant r means evidence of a linear relationship.
Conceptual takeaway: F for variance equality between two normals; correlation significance is a separate t-based check that ρ ≠ 0.
4.2.6.sourceQuote: The F-test, developed by Snedecor and Cochran (1983), is used to determine if the variances of two populations are equal.
4.2.6.compare: F-test here compares two variances; ANOVA uses F to compare several means via mean squares.

4.2.7.title: ANOVA for Fixed Effect Model
4.2.7.quick: Fixed-effect ANOVA models a response as treatment mean (or overall mean + fixed treatment effect) plus error, to compare mean responses across fixed treatments.
keyIdeas: Response = f(factor) + error; natural variation always remains even under similar settings.
Means model: yij = μi + εij — compare average response across treatments (e.g., fuel types’ mpg).
Effects model: yij = μ + τi + εij — overall mean plus ith treatment effect.
εij assumed identical, independent, normally distributed.
Error sources: experimental (treatment / stochastic EU / selection) and observational (measurement / sampling).
detail: The fuel-economy research question asks whether average mpg differs by fuel type; the means model generalises sample treatment means to the population and is linear in μ.

Isolating additive effects from a base response yields the effects form with τi. Earlier “variance analysis” business examples (material/labour/overhead) illustrate deviation-from-plan thinking, but the fixed-effect ANOVA core is the means/effects models above.
4.2.7.sourceQuote: The model is referred to as the means model since it is based on the mean treatment effect.
4.2.7.example: Fuel types as treatments; response = mpg; ask if mean mpg differs across fuels.

4.2.8.title: Total, Treatment & Error Sum of Squares
4.2.8.quick: ANOVA partitions variability into SSE (error), SSTR (treatment), and SST (total), then forms MSE/MSTR for the F test statistic.
keyIdeas: After SSE, compute SSTR and SST; then MSE and MSTR for the test statistic.
SSTR measures how much treatment means differ (e.g., battery-type lifetimes).
Low SSTR → treatment averages are similar.
SSTR steps: for each treatment, (column mean − grand mean)² × n_column.
SST = SSTR + SSE.
detail: Battery example: three types × four batteries; grand mean 2.1; column means 2.3, 1.85, 2.15 — SSTR from squared deviations times 4 per column; SST is SSTR + SSE.
Conceptual role: treatment SS captures between-group structure; error SS captures within-group noise; their mean squares feed the ANOVA F.
4.2.8.sourceQuote: The total sum of squares (SST) equals the sum of the SSTR and the SSE.

4.2.9.title: ANOVA for Random Effect Model
4.2.9.quick: Random-effect / two-factor (randomised block) ANOVA adds a blocking factor so units are grouped; treatments of interest are compared within more homogeneous blocks.
keyIdeas: Two-way factorial expands one-factor work with a second factor often used as blocks.
Compiler example: better to run the same programmes on each compiler (blocks) than assign different programmes to each.
Assumptions (one obs per cell): approximate normality per cell; common variance σ²; no interaction (effect of one factor consistent across levels of the other).
Interaction example: sugar × stirring on tea sweetness — stirring matters only with sugar.
Two-factor table: SSR (rows), SSC (columns), SSE with df (r−1)(c−1), F = MSR/MSE and MSC/MSE.
detail: Design (2) — four copies of five programmes, one per compiler — avoids confounding programme difficulty with compiler speed and yields a randomised block layout.
When interaction cannot be estimated (single observation per cell), the material assumes no interaction; sugar/stirring shows what interaction means conceptually.
4.2.9.sourceQuote: Therefore, it is sometimes referred to as a blocking factor as it categorises topics or units into similar groupings known as blocks. The design is referred to as a randomised block design.
4.2.9.compare: Fixed effects: specific treatment levels of interest; random/block structures control nuisance variation across units.

4.2.10.title: Single Factor Experiment
4.2.10.quick: A single-factor experiment varies levels of one independent factor to study its effect on a response; CRD randomly assigns treatments to homogeneous units.
keyIdeas: Popular designs: CRD, randomised block, Latin square, balanced incomplete block.
CRD: no grouping; allocate v treatments randomly; flexible unequal replications; all unit variability → error.
CRD suited to homogeneous material, labs, small numbers of treatments; often inefficient outdoors.
Model: yij = μ + τi + εij; H0: all τi = 0; SSTreatments (a−1 df) vs SSE (N−a df).
Lambs/diets illustration: fail to reject equal diet effects when F is small / p large.
detail: CRD layout: divide into n units, fix replications, randomly assign treatments without local control beyond choosing homogeneous units.
SSTreatments measures differences among treatment means; SSE is within-treatment random error with E(MSE) = σ². The diet example ends with F0 = 0.77 and fail to reject H0.
4.2.10.sourceQuote: Frequently we wish to investigate the effect of a factor (independent variable) on a response (dependent variable). Then we carried out an experiment where the levels of the factor are varied. Such an experiment is known as a single-factor experiment.
4.2.10.example: Four treatments on 20 units with unequal replications (3, 5, 6, 6) under CRD.

4.2.11.title: Model Adequacy Checking
4.2.11.quick: Model adequacy checking verifies regression assumptions (linearity, zero-mean errors, constant variance, independence, normality) mainly via residual diagnostics.
keyIdeas: Assumptions: roughly linear study–explanatory link; E(error)=0; constant variance; uncorrelated errors; normal errors.
Minor violations may be tolerable; major ones can make the model unstable across samples.
One predictor: scatter plot of y vs X for linearity.
Multiple predictors: scatter-plot matrix (off-diagonal plots; optional correlations).
Residual ei = yi − ŷi; residuals should reveal assumption failures; OLS residuals have mean zero.
detail: Assumptions are about the population while we observe a sample, so diagnostics on residuals (graphical) are the practical bridge.
Residuals quantify how far the fit misses the data and act as realised errors; examining them exposes model shortcomings.
4.2.11.sourceQuote: The residual is outlined because of the distinction between the discovered and fitted worth of study variable.

5.1.1.title: Meaning of Research Report
5.1.1.quick: A research report is a formal, structured document that records an investigation and reaches impartial conclusions; workplaces treat reports as legal papers.
keyIdeas: Three defining traits: predefined structure, independent sections, unbiased conclusions.
Structure headers (introduction, discussion, conclusion) guide the reader.
Sections can be read selectively without requiring a top-to-bottom read.
detail: The module opens by defining a report as a formal document used across sciences, social sciences, engineering, and business — essentially documenting the process of pursuing a defined assignment.
At a basic level, report writing is characterised by a predefined structure, independently written sections, and unbiased (impartial, objective) conclusions.
Independent sections matter because readers often jump to the parts they need rather than reading the whole report linearly.
5.1.1.sourceQuote: There are three fundamental characteristics that define report writing at a basic level:
5.1.1.compare: Unlike informal notes or opinion pieces, a research report is expected to be structured, sectionally independent, and objective.

5.1.2.title: Structure of Scientific Report
5.1.2.quick: A scientific report has preliminaries (title, TOC, etc.), contents (introduction; analysis/results), and reference materials (references, appendices, glossary, index).
keyIdeas: Preliminaries: title page, preface/acknowledgements, graphs/illustrations/tables/charts, table of contents.
Introduction covers aims, problem characterisation, hypotheses, concepts, literature, scope/assumptions/limitations, sampling, and methods.
Analysis presents factual results, quantitative analysis, summary and suggested actions; reference block holds refs, appendices, glossary, index.
detail: Preliminaries frame the document before the main narrative: title page, preface or foreword and acknowledgements, visuals lists, and table of contents.

The introduction is where aims, problem definition, hypotheses, key concepts, literature review, survey logistics (time/location/resources), scope/assumptions/limitations, sampling organisation, and data-collection approaches belong.

Results analysis covers type/volume/dimensions of findings, quantitative analysis, and a summary with suggested actions. Reference materials close with references, appendices (surveys, tables), glossary, and index.

5.1.3.title: Components of a Scientific Report
5.1.3.quick: A technical scientific report emphasises methods and sample design for peer academics: nature of work, methodology, data analysis, findings, bibliography, technical appendices.
keyIdeas: Written mainly for other academics; techniques and sample design must be well elucidated.
Main search/contents often limited to two or three pages; findings may span several chapters with tables/figures.
Bibliography lists secondary sources; technical appendices hold surveys, derivations, detailed methods.
detail: Technical reports differ in emphasis: colleagues care most about techniques used, and the extent of the search is tied to those strategies.

Core components include a short main-contents overview; nature of the research (objectives, operational problem, working hypothesis, analysis type, data required); research methodology with constraints (e.g. sample size/selection); data analysis covering sources, qualities, limits, and collection procedures for surveys; findings presentation with corroborating tables/figures; bibliography; and technical appendices.
5.1.3.sourceQuote: A technical report is primarily intended for other academics and, as such, may be structured in a fundamentally different manner.
5.1.3.compare: Technical reports stress methods and sample design; non-technical audiences (e.g. finance heads) often want outcomes, not process (see Types of Reports).

5.1.4.title: Types of Reports
5.1.4.quick: Reports are oral or written; written forms vary by time interval and by type (short/long, formal/informal, technical/non-technical, government).
keyIdeas: Oral reports demand live interaction, careful planning of what/how/how much to say, and Q&A readiness.
Written reports: short (narrow issue, ~5 pages e.g. monthly sales) vs long (technical + non-technical fusion).
Technical reports detail sources, methods, sample, tools, analysis, appendix, conclusions; non-technical focus on managerial implications.
detail: Oral presentation structure: opening (project nature, origins, objectives), findings/conclusions backed by evidence, suggestions tied to conclusions, then Q&A; visuals and tabular stats help. Prefer notes-driven extempore over memorisation or dull manuscript reading.
Written categories by interval: daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly. By type: short, long, formal, informal, government.
Examples: formal — marketing head’s quarterly test-marketing report to VP; informal — shift log book; government — rural employment strategy in a five-year plan.
5.1.4.sourceQuote: There are two types of reports (1) Oral report (2) Written report
5.1.4.example: A monthly sales report spanning about five pages for a product in a specified area is a short written report.

5.1.5.title: Steps in Report Writing
5.1.5.quick: After choosing the report type, structure it as: title page, contents, executive summary, body, conclusions/recommendations, bibliography, appendix.
keyIdeas: Executive summary (1–2 pages): objectives, brief methodology, important findings, key results, conclusion — often all top executives read.
Body: introduction, methodology/approach, limitations/constraints, analysis and interpretation.
Appendix holds non-essential but supporting materials (questionnaires, cuttings, diagrams, interviewer instructions).
detail: Title page states subject and preparing individual/organisation. Table of contents lists divisions with chapter titles and page numbers (declaration through appendix).

The body introduction describes the decision issue and research purpose with organisational background; approach covers primary vs secondary data, instruments, sample size/plan, analysis method, exploratory vs conclusive design; constraints include time, geography, technique, response accuracy.
Conclusions answer what outcomes were drawn; recommendations answer what you advise based on the study. Bibliography lists secondary sources with title, journal, volume, pages, edition.
5.1.5.sourceQuote: Once the type of report has been determined, the subsequent stage is to prepare the report.

5.1.6.title: Format and Writing Style
5.1.6.quick: Physical layout creates first impression and navigability; style must simplify, justify with data, quantify, and inform rather than impress.
keyIdeas: Layout: strong title page/TOC, uniform margins/spacing, consistent heading fonts (e.g. 16–18 chapter, 14 section, 12 subsection), quality print, numbered figures/tables, precise citations.
Readers are short on time, busy, and often unfamiliar with research jargon.
Prefer short sentences, active voice, logical presentation; avoid exaggeration and vague passives.
detail: A well-formed physical layout creates a favourable first impression, shows organisational structure, and lets readers choose which section to read first.

Style rules from the extract: simplify to essentials; justify every statement with facts/data; quantify (say 50% or one in three, not 'large'/'small'); be precise; inform not impress; use short sentences and spare adjectives; avoid passive voice that creates vagueness; stay logical and systematic.
5.1.6.sourceQuote: Justify. Make no statement that is not based on facts and data.

5.1.7.title: Illustrations and Tables
5.1.7.quick: Tables/figures need consistent titles/captions, legible text (≥2 mm), sequential numbering, and consistent placement; copyrighted material needs replacement notices.
keyIdeas: Number sequentially through the thesis or as chapter.item (Table 1.1); never mix styles (Table 1 with Figure 1.3).
Placement options: after first mention, end of chapter, or before bibliography — pick one and stay consistent.
After reduction, lettering must remain readable; long reports use separate Lists of Figures/Tables.
detail: Designate items as Table/Figure (etc.) with title/caption included in the relevant list; replicate headings on continued multi-page tables and break at sensible subheading boundaries.
If a caption cannot fit on the same page as the visual, put it on a separate page. If visuals are grouped at the end, TOC must point to that location.
For excluded copyrighted visuals: assert removal due to copyright, describe the material (with link if available), and give the full original reference.
5.1.7.sourceQuote: Regardless of the chosen technique, the numbering style must be consistent for all numbered items.

5.1.8.title: Citing and Referencing Sources
5.1.8.quick: Numerical footnotes map to a consecutive reference list; bibliography entries follow Harvard-like formatting; use Op. cit., Loc. cit., and Ibid. for repeats.
keyIdeas: List only publications actually referenced; title the section 'References' rather than 'Bibliography' when that is the case.
Op. cit. = work previously cited (author, date, page as needed); Loc. cit. = same page previously cited; Ibid. = same work as immediately before.
Abbreviations avoid full duplication when the same source is cited repeatedly.
detail: Footnote numbers in text (e.g. after 'Recent studies suggest that…') correspond directly to the reference list ordered as cited.
Individual citation formatting inside the bibliography mirrors the Harvard method described in the extract.
5.1.8.sourceQuote: The section should be titled ‘References’ instead of ‘Bibliography’, as indicated below.
5.1.8.compare: Footnotes (5.1.9) identify quoted materials and add supplementary notes; the reference list records the cited works.

5.1.9.title: Footnotes
5.1.9.quick: Footnotes identify quoted materials and add supplementary value (cross-refs, authorities, acknowledgements, elucidation); they are not a display of scholarship.
keyIdeas: Two purposes: correct identification of quoted materials; supplementary value to the main body.
Enable cross-references, citation of authorities/sources, acknowledgement, and explanation of a point of view.
Recent trend is to avoid footnotes; they are neither an end nor a means of displaying scholarship.
detail: Researchers insert footnotes at appropriate places. A numbered cue such as after 'Recent research indicates that…' points to the references.
The extract cautions against treating footnotes as proof of scholarly display.
5.1.9.sourceQuote: The footnotes provide supplementary value to the main part(body) of the text.

5.2.1.title: Oral Presentation
5.2.1.quick: Oral presentation is harder than written reporting because of live audience interaction; plan content, delivery, volume, visuals, and Q&A.
keyIdeas: Opening states project nature, how it arose, and what was attempted; conclusions backed by findings; recommendations supported by conclusions.
Prefer expanding from concise notes (extempore) over memorisation or monotonous manuscript reading.
Use simple language, strict time management, charts/graphs, circulated vital figures, audience knowledge, and purpose (decision vs information).
detail: Any delay can leave a negative impression and undermine presenter confidence. Communication decisions — what/how/how much to say — and facing audience questions require substantial preparation.
Method of presentation: use visuals when needed; tabular form helps statistical information. Logical sequencing is required.
5.2.1.sourceQuote: It’s more difficult to prepare as compared to the written report.

5.2.2.title: Making Presentation
5.2.2.quick: Golden rule: human attention is limited — one idea per slide, clear intro and last-slide conclusions, rehearse aloud (≥5 times for important talks), never go overtime.
keyIdeas: Organisation: strategic (non-technical) introduction; mention companion paper for details; periodic outline slides; sequential unifying thread; less is better.
Mechanics: PowerPoint preferred (avoid LaTeX except formulas); humour only if natural; listen carefully to questions asked.
Text: short titles, little text, no small fonts, few formulas/code; Illustrations: prefer pictures, restrained animation, strong vs pastel colour roles.
detail: Do not put slides after the conclusion slide — that weakens impact. Do not expect the audience to remember colour-coding across slides; restate if needed.
Give a high-level overview before details so listeners can relate details to the big picture and save attention for later important parts.
Spell-check: a spelling mistake is an 'attention magnet'. Don't explain the completely obvious; don't treat the audience as impaired.
5.2.2.sourceQuote: Human attention is extremely limited. Don’t cram an excessive amount of information, either in each slide, or within the whole talk.

5.2.3.title: Use of Visual Aids
5.2.3.quick: Visual aids (graphs, photos, video, slides, whiteboard, handouts, flip chart, posters) summarise, clarify, emphasise, engage — one key point per aid; ensure the talk still works without them.
keyIdeas: Purposes: summarise/reduce spoken words, clarify with examples, emphasise, make memorable, enhance credibility, engage, ease understanding.
During delivery: visible to all, don't read from the aid, explain immediately when shown, hide when unused.
PowerPoint tips include ≥24pt font, simple background, purposeful animation only, avoid red/green text, one key point per slide.
detail: Preparation: support the spoken message, avoid clutter, keep style consistent, use graphs/charts for data, moderate use for essential points only.

Handouts: partially completed sheets force listening; giving full handouts too early causes reading instead of listening. Whiteboards suit process diagrams and persistent key definitions. Flip charts suit small audiences/brainstorming. Posters are portable but can be costly if complex. Videos: relevant, as short as needed, announce duration.
5.2.3.sourceQuote: One message per visual aid, for example, on a slide there should only be one key point.

5.2.4.title: Importance of Effective Communication
5.2.4.quick: Effective communication (attentive listening, empathy, open-mindedness, helpful feedback, confident nonverbal cues) builds trust, prevents/resolves conflict, clarifies direction, and boosts engagement and productivity.
keyIdeas: Benefits listed: building trust; preventing/resolving problems; providing clarity and direction; better relationships; increases engagement; improves productivity; promotes team building.
Cited engagement study note: only 15% of adult employees engaged with employers — communication can raise engagement/satisfaction.
Clarity includes constructive correction and clear roles to eliminate confusion.
detail: Leaders who communicate well see better productivity and improved relationships at work and in personal life.
Conflict resolution depends on remaining calm, ensuring all parties are heard, and finding an ideal solution for everyone involved.
When roles and expectations are clear, people focus on work rather than workplace issues; conflicts resolve faster and distractions shrink.
5.2.4.sourceQuote: Effective communication involves knowing how to listen attentively. It’s the ability to offer empathy, open-mindedness, and helpful feedback.

5.2.5.title: Convention and Strategies of Authentication
5.2.5.quick: Authenticate reports by interpreting tables (not dumping all cell numbers), using qualitative quotes with scientific value, and avoiding careless/outdated/unsupported content.
keyIdeas: Pitfall: endless description without interpretation — tables need conclusions.
Qualitative quotes illustrate findings and let readers draw conclusions (avoid biased selection).
Avoid: inaccurate/conflicting data; outdated/irrelevant data; unseparated facts vs opinions; unsupported conclusions; careless proofreading; appearance over content.
detail: Coding open opinions as mere counts without interpretation is called a serious maltreatment of data that needs correction — qualitative material can illustrate reasons and attitudes.
Authentication here means making the report trustworthy: interpret evidence, separate fact from opinion, and support proposals.
5.2.5.sourceQuote: Tables need conclusions, not detailed presentation of all numbers or percentages within the cells which readers can see for themselves.

5.3.1.title: Preparing Research Papers for Journals
5.3.1.quick: Journal preparation is a multi-step pipeline from authorship planning and early writing through peer review, proofs, and celebration of publication as completing the experiment.
keyIdeas: Three peer-reviewed formats: full-length (IMRaD), short/brief (~≤3500 words, ≤2 tables/figures), rapid communications for 'hot' findings.
Do not compromise on peer review when selecting a journal; consider language, focus, indexing, availability, reputation/IF, format, figures, time-to-print, charges.
Build figures/tables before writing; revise in order: major alterations → polish style → format; answer every reviewer comment on resubmission.
detail: Start writing before experiments finish — writing evokes new ideas for controls/experiments. Publish when findings form a complete, significant contribution.
Stock Introduction/Methods/Results/Discussion folders; outline as a roadmap; assign co-author sections but edit to one voice.
Robert Day: a spectacular experiment is not complete until results are published.
5.3.1.sourceQuote: The goal of scientific research is publication…. A particular experiment, no matter how spectacular the results, is not complete until the results are published.

5.3.2.title: Design of Paper Using Template
5.3.2.quick: Use a hierarchical outline template: Introduction (background + thesis), sequenced main points with sub-points and supported examples, critical-thinking section, then conclusion affirming the thesis.
keyIdeas: No fixed letter/number count — structure follows how many points the paper length requires.
Never start a sentence with an unintroduced quotation.
Critical thinking section: reactions to sources, insights, synthesise threads; conclusion affirms the thesis is proven.
detail: First main point expands via sub-points, each with corresponding examples/details (insight or critic paraphrase/quote) plus supporting comments; continue alternating numerals and letters for further main points.
The template keeps the argument operationally organised rather than free-form.
5.3.2.sourceQuote: Notice that no correct number of letters or numbers exists; the sole determining factor is the number of points we need to create for the specified length of our paper.

5.3.3.title: Calculation of Impact Factor of a Journal
5.3.3.quick: Journal impact factor (IF) for a year = citations in that year to items published in the prior two years, divided by the count of citable items in those two years.
keyIdeas: IF measures how often the average article in a journal is cited in a given year — used to rank importance within a category.
Example form: 2010 IF = A/B where A = 2010 cites to 2008–2009 articles; B = citable items published 2008–2009.
Rule of thumb in extract: IF ≥10 excellent, ~3 good, average <1 — compare journals within the same category.
detail: Calculation is based on a two-year period: divide times articles were cited by the number of citable articles.
Cross-category IF comparisons are less meaningful than within-field comparisons.
5.3.3.example: If indexed journals cite 2008–2009 articles 500 times in 2010 and there were 100 citable items in 2008–2009, IF ≈ 5.0.

5.3.4.title: Citation Index
5.3.4.quick: A citation index is a bibliographic database of citations between publications, showing which later documents cite earlier ones; citation count is how often an article is cited.
keyIdeas: Major services: ISI/Thomson Reuters Web of Science (SCI, SSCI, A&HCI, etc.) and Elsevier Scopus.
Other databases: CiteSeer, RePEc, Google Scholar, EBSCOhost, Compendex.
Indian Citation Index (ICI) covers ~1000 Indian scholarly journals across disciplines and produces ISCI, ISSHCI, IJCR, ISTA, DOIJ.
detail: A scientifically written article lists references serially; each reference is a citation. Citation indexes let users establish later→earlier citation links.
Scopus is described as among the largest abstract/citation databases of peer-reviewed literature with tools to track citations.
5.3.4.sourceQuote: A citation index could be a kind of bibliographic database, an index of citations between publications, allowing the user to simply establish which later documents cite which earlier documents

5.3.5.title: ISBN and ISSN
5.3.5.quick: ISBN identifies individual books/volumes (now 13-digit; mandatory where applicable); ISSN identifies serials/series (8-digit; optional) and stays the same across issues of a series.
keyIdeas: ISBN = International Standard Book Number; ISSN = International Standard Serial Number.
ISBN identifies publisher context for a monograph; ISSN does not identify the publisher the same way.
ISSN drafted 1971; assigned by National Centres, coordinated by ISSN International Centre in Paris.
detail: History: Gordon Foster's nine-digit code → ISO ten-digit → after 2007, 13-digit ISBN. Different formats (hardback, PDF, EPUB) get different ISBNs.
When a series changes, another ISSN is allotted; all volumes of one series share the same ISSN.
5.3.5.sourceQuote: “ISBN” stands for “International Standard Book Number” whereas “ISSN” is “International Standard Serial Number.”
5.3.5.compare: ISBN differs per volume/issue; ISSN is identical across volumes of one series.

5.4.1.title: Identifying and Defining Problem
5.4.1.quick: Selecting and properly defining the research problem is the first step; a research problem is a situation needing description, explanation, or prediction of a solution.
keyIdeas: Like a doctor, examine all symptoms before diagnosing the problem correctly.
Components: a person/group with difficulty; objectives; alternative means; doubt about relative efficiency of alternatives; an environment of the difficulty.
Problem selection often hard not from scarcity of topics but from finding socially relevant work without duplicating earlier studies; may identify a knowledge gap.
detail: Identifying a research problem refers to difficulty in a theoretical or practical situation seeking a solution — the focus or reason for the research.
Defining the problem drives the scientific process and underpins method and experimental design.
5.4.1.sourceQuote: Research problem: A situation or circumstances that require a solution to be described, explained or predicted.

5.4.2.title: Research Problem Aspects and Considerations
5.4.2.quick: Define a problem by stating it within clear study bounds: statement, nature/origin, literature survey, deduction from theory, then rephrase into an operational working proposition.
keyIdeas: Aspects: (i) statement of the problem (ii) understanding nature/origin (iii) surveying available literature (iv) deduction from theory (v) rephrasing into a working proposition.
Broad general questions are usually unsuitable for testing until narrowed operationally.
Considerations: identify concepts/terms in the topic; review related literature (incl. multidisciplinary databases); use additional sources to strengthen arguments.
detail: Literature survey reveals available vs required materials, theory gaps, inconsistent theories, or findings that break theoretical expectations — enabling new strides from existing premises.
Related studies flag likely difficulties and analytical shortcomings and may suggest new approaches. Do not define the problem hurriedly.
A research guide can help consider problems carefully.
5.4.2.sourceQuote: Defining a research problem properly and clearly is a crucial part of a research study and must in no case be accomplished hurriedly.

5.4.3.title: Research Plan
5.4.3.quick: A research plan is the blueprint for resolving the defined problem: design, collect, interpret, and report — alongside proposal planning (objectives, scope, feasibility, work plan, budget, risk, stakeholders, metrics).
keyIdeas: Locate/define issues with purpose, background, needed information, and decision use.
Design steps include secondary data, qualitative analysis, quantitative methods, data definition, measurement/scaling, questionnaire, sampling, analysis strategy.

Collect via interviews, observation, questionnaires, focus groups, documents; interpret by ordering findings then drafting conclusions; report via formal paper, article, PowerPoint, A/V, spreadsheet — plus oral presentation with tables/figures/graphs.
detail: Proposal planning also covers defining objectives, identifying scope (prevent creep), feasibility (technical/financial/operational), work plan/milestones/roles, budgeting, risk management, stakeholder engagement, evaluation metrics, documentation, and review/revision.
Field collection examples: in-home/mall/CAPI, telephone/CATI, traditional mail and mail panels.
5.4.3.sourceQuote: A research plan or approach is a blueprint or framework for carrying out a marketing research project.
